name: Question 4
problem: Find the first three non-zero terms of the Taylor expansion of $x\operatorname{cos}⁡\pi x$ about $x=1.$
worked_solution:
We use Taylor's theorem in the form

$$
f(x)=f(a)+{f}^{′}(a)(x-a)+\frac{{f}^{″}(a)}{2!}(x-a)^{2}+\frac{{f}^{‴}(a)}{3!}(x-a)^{3}+⋯,
$$

with $f(x)=x\operatorname{cos}⁡\pi x$ and $a=1.$ 

Computing the required derivatives, we have

$$
\begin{aligned}f(x) & =x\operatorname{cos}⁡\pi x \\ f(1) & =(1)\operatorname{cos}⁡\pi =-1 \\ {f}^{′}(x) & =\operatorname{cos}⁡\pi x-\pi x\operatorname{sin}⁡\pi x \\ {f}^{′}(1) & =\operatorname{cos}⁡\pi -(1)\pi \operatorname{sin}⁡\pi =-1+0=-1 \\ {f}^{″}(x) & =-\pi \operatorname{sin}⁡\pi x-\pi \operatorname{sin}⁡\pi x-{\pi }^{2}x\operatorname{cos}⁡\pi x=-2\pi \operatorname{sin}⁡\pi x-{\pi }^{2}x\operatorname{cos}⁡\pi x \\ {f}^{″}(1) & =-2\pi \operatorname{sin}⁡\pi -{\pi }^{2}(1)\operatorname{cos}⁡\pi =0+{\pi }^{2}={\pi }^{2}.\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore,

$$
\begin{aligned}x\operatorname{cos}⁡\pi x & =-1-(x-1)+\frac{{\pi }^{2}}{2!}(x-1)^{2}+⋯ \\  & =-1-(x-1)+\frac{{\pi }^{2}}{2}(x-1)^{2}+⋯.\end{aligned}
$$

Find the first three non-zero terms of the Taylor expansion of xcos⁡πx about x=1.

a
 xcos⁡πx=−1+12(x−1)−π23(x−1)2+⋯
b
 xcos⁡πx=(x−1)−(x−1)2+π22(x−1)3+⋯
c
 xcos⁡πx=−1+2(x−1)−π22(x−1)2+⋯
d
 xcos⁡πx=(x−1)+12(x−1)2−π24(x−1)3+⋯
e
 xcos⁡πx=−1−(x−1)+π22(x−1)2+⋯
Submit
Incorrect
EXPLANATION

We use Taylor's theorem in the form f(x)=f(a)+f′(a)(x−a)+f″(a)2!(x−a)2+f‴(a)3!(x−a)3+⋯, with f(x)=xcos⁡πx and a=1.

Computing the required derivatives, we have

f(x)=xcos⁡πxf(1)=(1)cos⁡π=−1f′(x)=cos⁡πx−πxsin⁡πxf′(1)=cos⁡π−(1)πsin⁡π=−1+0=−1f″(x)=−πsin⁡πx−πsin⁡πx−π2xcos⁡πx=−2πsin⁡πx−π2xcos⁡πxf″(1)=−2πsin⁡π−π2(1)cos⁡π=0+π2=π2.

Therefore,

xcos⁡πx=−1−(x−1)+π22!(x−1)2+⋯=−1−(x−1)+π22(x−1)2+⋯.
